departments.name: Police & Animal Control
departments.blurb: Patrol, investigations, the 911 dispatch contract, records and animal control.
departments.cutNarrative: Slower response times, thinner patrol coverage overnight, longer case backlogs. The $1.1M dispatch contract is fixed, so cuts land on sworn staffing.
departments.raiseNarrative: Supports the proposed staffing plan. Funding a position is not the same as filling it — the unit was already carrying vacancies it was recruiting for.

staffing.scopeNote: Spans sworn police, records and support, and animal control. Most vacancies were sworn officers; no exact count given.

proposal.label: Proposed target
proposal.text: Continue recruiting for seven Police positions.
proposal.caveat: A proposal from the June 16, 2026 budget discussion — not adopted hires, and not a guarantee any post gets filled.

departments.blurb: Fire suppression, medical first response, prevention and inspection.
departments.cutNarrative: Constant staffing is what fire costs. Cut it and you brown out an engine company or pay the difference back in overtime.

departments.name: Administrative Services
departments.blurb: Finance, HR, IT and risk. Also where the overdue audits live.
departments.cutNarrative: Thinner finance staff. The overdue audits slip further, which lenders notice.
departments.raiseNarrative: Staffs up finance to clear the audit backlog and rebuild bank reconciliations.

departments.name: Community Development & Engineering
departments.blurb: Planning, building inspection, permits and engineering. Carries $3.7M of permit revenue with it.
departments.cutNarrative: Permit turnaround slows, which quietly drags on the $3.7M of building permit revenue this department collects.
departments.raiseNarrative: Faster permits and inspections; development revenue picks up.

departments.name: Non-Departmental & Contingency
departments.blurb: Citywide legal, audit, insurance, memberships — and a $1.2M contingency.
departments.cutNarrative: The contingency is the first thing to go and the thing you miss when a pump station fails in March.
departments.raiseNarrative: Rebuilds the contingency and funds the audit catch-up.

departments.name: City Manager, Clerk & Council
departments.blurb: Executive office, the clerk, elections and the city's events budget.
departments.cutNarrative: Small money. Residents read cuts here as the city taking its own medicine first.
departments.raiseNarrative: More executive capacity for the loan agreements and labour negotiations ahead.

departments.name: Public Works & Streets
departments.blurb: The General Fund's share of streets, facilities and solid waste. Most of Public Works sits in the water, sewer and gas tax funds.
departments.cutNarrative: Pothole backlog grows and the pavement condition index keeps sliding.
departments.raiseNarrative: Clears the pothole backlog and resumes the slurry seal program.

departments.name: Parks & Recreation
departments.blurb: Parks maintenance, youth and senior programs, pool, community events.
departments.cutNarrative: Reduced program hours, browner turf, shorter pool season. The most visible cut on this list.
departments.raiseNarrative: Restores youth programming and park maintenance cycles.

generalFund.deficitLabel: Adopted FY 2026-27 General Fund budget gap
generalFund.gapNote: The difference between the adopted budget’s expenditure and revenue totals. The game does not classify the City’s own lines as recurring or one-time — some include contingency and capital spending — so this is the adopted gap, not a verified structural deficit.

projection.note: Growth assumptions for the five-year outlook. A game estimate built on the rates below, not a City forecast, and not a verified structural projection: the adopted revenue and expenditure lines have never been classified recurring or one-time.
projection.expenditureGrowthNote: Personnel is $34.95M of a $56.59M General Fund. Salary steps, CalPERS rate increases and insurance renewals outrun revenue growth. This is the structural problem.

revisedDeficit.label: Later revised figure
revisedDeficit.note: The General Fund budget-to-actual report published after adoption shows expenses revised up to $57,149,450 against the same $50,224,900 of revenue, widening the gap from $6,363,284 to $6,924,550. The City's own October 2026 infographic carries this $6.9M figure. The game is played on the adopted budget; this is shown alongside it, not instead of it.

sources.title: A Clear Look At Our Financial Situation

revisedDeficit.labelDiscrepancy: The City infographic captions these figures "Adopted Budget FY 2025-26" and "July - September 2025", but the amounts ($50.2M revenue, $57.1M expenses, $6.9M gap) match the FY 2026-27 budget-to-actual exactly. Reproduced here as published.
